title: Microexpressions
description: Incredibly fast, involuntary facial twitches that reveal a concealed emotion.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A microexpression is a lightning-fast facial movement (lasting less than a fifth of a second) that unintentionally leaks a person's true emotion before their conscious brain can cover it up with a socially acceptable fake expression.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: A split-second flash of anger quickly replaced by a bright smile.
A sudden, tiny tightening of the lips before speaking nicely.
A momentary wrinkling of the nose in disgust.
A brief flash of fear in the eyes that vanishes instantly.

sections.title: What It May Indicate
content: Concealed emotions they do not want you to see.
Suppressed anger, disgust, fear, sadness, contempt, surprise, or joy.
A subconscious, visceral reaction directly conflicting with their spoken words.

sections.title: What It Does NOT Mean
content: A microexpression does NOT prove someone is lying. It only proves they are feeling an emotion they are actively trying to hide.
A twitch is NOT always a microexpression. Sometimes a facial twitch is literally just a muscle spasm.

sections.title: Real Life Examples
content: Negotiation: You name your price, and the buyer flashes a microexpression of joy (a tiny smirk) before acting deeply disappointed. They love the price.
Workplace: Your boss smiles and congratulates you, but a split-second sneer of contempt flashes on their face first.
Argument: Someone claims they 'aren't mad', but their lips quickly thin and tighten into anger for a millisecond.

sections.title: Cluster Analysis
content: Microexpression of fear + sudden freezing posture + throat clearing = High stress / Panic.
Fake smile + microexpression of disgust = Polite but strong internal rejection.
Microexpression of anger + clenched fists + leaning forward = Suppressed hostility.

sections.title: Common Situations
content: High-stakes business negotiations.
Police interrogations.
Difficult relationship conversations.
Poker games.

sections.title: Observation Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Believing microexpressions are a magical, foolproof lie detector. Reality: They only tell you *what* someone is feeling, not *why* they are feeling it, or if they are explicitly lying about the facts.

sections.title: Practical Observation Tips
content: Do not stare exclusively at their face like a laser. Keep a soft, broad gaze on the entire person to catch movements.
Watch for asymmetry. Fake emotions are often slightly lopsided. Real microexpressions, especially contempt (a one-sided smirk), flash precisely.
Pay attention to the exact timing. If the facial expression is delayed a full second after the emotional event, it is likely faked.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Seeing an emotion completely opposite to what the person is claiming (e.g., claiming to be devastated, but flashing a microexpression of joy, known as 'duping delight').
A flash of 'contempt' built directly into a supposedly friendly interaction.
A face that quickly shifts through three different emotions in under a second.

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: Microexpressions are incredibly hard to catch in real-time. Even highly trained professionals miss them constantly. If you think you saw one, treat it solely as a hint to ask better questions, not as a final judgment of character or legal guilt.
